title: Magnetic Field Intensity
short_intro: Magnetic field intensity (often denoted by H or magnetic field strength) is a vector field quantity that represents the magnitude of the magnetic field produced by external currents without taking into account the magnetization of the medium. Its SI unit is ampere per meter (A/m) and its dimensional formula is [M<sup>0</sup>L<sup>-1</sup>T<sup>0</sup>A<sup>1</sup>].

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition of magnetic field intensity, Biot-Savart Law, Ampere's Circuital Law, magnetic field due to straight conductor, circular coil, and long solenoid.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Relation between B, H, and M (B = μ<sub>0</sub>(H + M)), magnetic susceptibility, hysteresis loops, toroid calculations, and boundary conditions for magnetic fields across interfaces.

prerequisites: Concept of electric current and current density
Fundamental magnetic forces and Lorentz force

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Physical Significance of H
bullets: Magnetic field intensity H is defined as the magnetic field produced by free or conduction currents alone.
It is independent of the magnetic properties of the medium through which it passes.
The total magnetic induction B inside a medium is the sum of the external field contribution (μ<sub>0</sub>H) and the material's magnetization contribution (μ<sub>0</sub>M).

concept_notes.heading: Biot-Savart Law
bullets: Provides the differential magnetic field dB at a point due to a current-element Idl.
The direction of dB is given by the right-hand thumb rule for cross product of Idl and position vector r.

concept_notes.heading: Ampere's Circuital Law
bullets: States that the line integral of magnetic field intensity H around any closed loop is equal to the total free current enclosed by the loop.
Expressed mathematically as ∮ H · dl = I<sub>free, enclosed</sub>.
Particularly useful for highly symmetric systems such as solenoids, toroids, and straight current-carrying cylinders.

concept_notes.heading: Relation Between B, H, and Magnetization M
bullets: The constitutive relation in magnetism is given by B = μ<sub>0</sub>(H + M).
Magnetization M is defined as the magnetic dipole moment per unit volume of the material.
For linear isotropic media, M = χ<sub>m</sub>H, leading to B = μ<sub>0</sub>(1 + χ<sub>m</sub>)H = μH, where χ<sub>m</sub> is magnetic susceptibility and μ is magnetic permeability.

derivations.title: Magnetic Field Intensity Inside a Long Solenoid
derivations.conditions: Infinitely long solenoid, tightly wound with n turns per unit length carrying current I.
steps: Consider a rectangular Amperean loop of length l, with one side parallel to the axis inside the solenoid and the opposite side far outside where the field is zero.
Apply Ampere's Circuital Law: ∮ H · dl = I<sub>enc</sub>.
The line integral evaluates only along the internal side of length l, since the perpendicular sides contribute zero and the external side experiences zero field.
Total enclosed free current I<sub>enc</sub> = n · l · I.
Equate the line integral to the enclosed current: H × l = n · l · I.

derivations.title: Magnetic Field Intensity at the Center of a Circular Current-Carrying Coil
derivations.conditions: Circular coil of radius R having N turns and carrying current I.
steps: Consider an infinitesimally small current element Idl on the circular loop.
Using the Biot-Savart law, the angle between Idl and position vector r is 90 degrees (sin θ = 1).
The differential magnetic induction is dB = (μ<sub>0</sub>/4π) * (I dl / R<sup>2</sup>).
Integrate around the entire circumference: B = ∫ dB = (μ<sub>0</sub>I / 4πR<sup>2</sup>) ∮ dl = (μ<sub>0</sub>I / 4πR<sup>2</sup>)(2πRN).
Convert magnetic induction B to magnetic field intensity H by dividing by μ<sub>0</sub> (in vacuum, H = B / μ<sub>0</sub>).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Hysteresis Loop (B vs H Curve)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A closed loop showing non-linear relationship between B and H during cyclic magnetization and demagnetization, marking retentivity and coercivity.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Area of the hysteresis loop represents thermal energy loss per unit volume per magnetization cycle in ferromagnetic materials.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested for identifying soft and hard ferromagnetic materials based on loop area, retentivity, and coercivity.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Magnetic Field Intensity H vs Distance r for a Long Straight Conductor
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A rectangular hyperbola curve showing H decreasing inversely with distance r (H ∝ 1/r).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the rapid fall-off of magnetic field intensity away from a linear current source.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual questions comparing field intensity at different radial distances from a cable.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Magnetization M vs Magnetic Field Intensity H
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Linear plots for paramagnetic (positive constant slope), diamagnetic (negative constant slope), and asymptotic/saturation curves for ferromagnetic materials.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The slope of M versus H yields the magnetic susceptibility χ_m of the material.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Numerical and theoretical questions regarding susceptibility calculations.

solved_numericals.question: A long solenoid of length 2.0 m has 2000 turns and carries a current of 1.5 A. Calculate the magnetic field intensity H inside the solenoid.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: Total turns N = 2000, Length L = 2.0 m, Current I = 1.5 A.
Calculate turns per unit length: n = N / L = 2000 / 2.0 = 1000 turns/m.
Use formula for magnetic field intensity of a solenoid: H = nI.
Substitute values: H = 1000 m<sup>-1</sup> × 1.5 A = 1500 A/m.

solved_numericals.question: A magnetic material is placed in an external magnetic field intensity H of 1000 A/m. If the resulting magnetization M is 3000 A/m, find the magnetic induction B and the magnetic susceptibility of the material.
solution_steps: Given: H = 1000 A/m, M = 3000 A/m, μ<sub>0</sub> = 4π × 10<sup>-7</sup> T·m/A.
Calculate magnetic susceptibility χ<sub>m</sub> using M = χ<sub>m</sub>H: χ<sub>m</sub> = M / H = 3000 / 1000 = 3.
Calculate magnetic induction B using B = μ<sub>0</sub>(H + M): B = (4π × 10<sup>-7</sup>) × (1000 + 3000).

solved_numericals.question: A circular coil of 50 turns and radius 0.1 m carries a current of 2.0 A. What is the magnetic field intensity at the center of the coil?
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: N = 50, R = 0.1 m, I = 2.0 A.
Use the formula for magnetic field intensity at the center of a circular coil: H = (NI) / (2R).

assumptions_and_limitations: Ampere's Circuital Law calculations assume high degree of symmetry (such as infinite length or closed toroidal geometry) to easily extract H from the line integral.
Biot-Savart Law assumes steady (time-independent) currents; for time-varying currents, displacement current contributions must be included via Maxwell-Ampere law.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Magnetic field intensity H depends directly on the magnetic properties (permeability) of the surrounding medium.
common_misconceptions.correct: Magnetic field intensity H depends solely on free/conduction currents and geometrical configuration, independent of the medium.
common_misconceptions.why: The medium's property (permeability μ or susceptibility χ_m) affects the magnetic induction B and magnetization M, but by definition, H is the auxiliary field generated purely by external free currents.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The SI unit of magnetic field intensity H is Tesla.
common_misconceptions.correct: The SI unit of H is Ampere per meter (A/m), whereas Tesla (T) is the unit of magnetic induction B.
common_misconceptions.why: Tesla measures magnetic flux density or induction, while H represents current per unit length driving the field.

quick_revision: Magnetic field intensity H has units of A/m and is produced exclusively by free currents.
Fundamental formula for a long solenoid is H = nI.
Constitutive relation connecting fields is B = μ<sub>0</sub>(H + M).
Magnetic susceptibility is defined by the relation M = χ<sub>m</sub>H.
